etymology: Saxon graedig, ravenous, hungry. In Ephesians 4:19 it renders the Greek pleonexia, the desire to have more — the same word the apostle elsewhere translates covetousness.
biblical_def: Paul describes the Gentile condition in a sentence that moves from numbness to appetite: “Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness” (Ephesians 4:19). The order matters. First the conscience goes dead — past feeling, the Greek word for a callus. Then the man hands himself over. Then the sin is worked, and worked with greediness. The Greek is pleonexia, the lust for more, which Paul names outright as idolatry: “and covetousness, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5). Uncleanness pursued greedily is not pleasure-seeking; it is worship directed at an appetite that never fills. The Authorized Version uses greediness once, and it names the engine of the old man — corrupt “according to the deceitful lusts” (Ephesians 4:22). Deceitful, because they promise satisfaction and produce a larger hunger. The remedy in the same chapter is not moderation but exchange: put off the old man and put on the new. Scripture never asks the greedy heart to want less; it asks it to be made new and to want God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): GREEDINESS, noun Ravenousness; voracity; keen appetite; eager desire of attainment.
webster_full: GREEDINESS, noun Keenness of appetite for food or drink; ravenousness; voracity.
2. Ardent desire; eagerness of attainment.
GREEDY, adjective Having a keen appetite for food or drink; ravenous; voracious; very hungry.
2. Having a keen desire of any thing; eager to obtain; as, greedy of gain.
3. In Scripture, covetous; eager for wealth, in a culpable degree.
scriptures: Eph 4:19
Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.
Eph 4:22
That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts;
Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
corruption_summary: Greediness is treated as an appetite disorder to be managed; Scripture names it covetousness, calls it idolatry, and prescribes mortification.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic account of this verse replaces the apostle's categories throughout. Past feeling becomes dissociation; given themselves over becomes compulsion; greediness becomes an unmet need. Each substitution moves the man from the dock to the couch. Paul's diagnosis is moral: the conscience is calloused, the will is complicit, and the appetite is an idol.

The principle to recover is that the cure is not restraint but regeneration. Ephesians 4 commands the putting off of the old man and the putting on of the new, and Colossians 3:5 commands mortification — killing, not managing. A desire that is idolatry cannot be made lawful by reducing its volume.

pos: n. (the quality of being red; here, the bloodshot eye of the drunkard)
etymology: Saxon read, red, with the abstract ending -ness. In Proverbs 23:29 it renders the Hebrew chaklilil, dark-flashing or bloodshot.
biblical_def: Solomon asks six questions and answers all of them with one word: “Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath babbling? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes?” (Proverbs 23:29). The answer comes in the next verse: “They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine” (Proverbs 23:30). The list is a clinical description — grief, quarrels, slurred speech, unexplained injuries, and bloodshot eyes — and Scripture puts the physical symptom last, as the visible sign of all the rest. The Authorized Version uses redness once, and it is a mercy that it does, because the wise man will not let the reader abstract the sin from the body that carries it. Then comes the command: “Look not thou upon the wine when it is red” (Proverbs 23:31). Not taste not merely — look not. The eye is where the sin begins and the eye is where it shows. Scripture nowhere forbids wine; it names drunkenness a work of the flesh and shows the drunkard's face as its own argument.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): REDNESS, noun The quality of being red; red color.
webster_full: REDNESS, noun The quality of being red; red color.
RED, adjective Of a bright color, resembling blood.
2. In Scripture, red is used of wine, of the eyes of the drunkard, and of the garments of the conqueror.
RED-EYED, adjective Having red eyes.
REDDISH, adjective Somewhat red; moderately red.
scriptures: Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions
They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine.
Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright.
corruption_summary: Drunkenness is widely reclassified as a disease only; Scripture calls it a work of the flesh with symptoms, and commands the eye away from the cup.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern settlement treats habitual drunkenness as a disease and nothing else. Scripture is more honest than that in both directions. It describes real bodily ruin — wounds, babbling, redness of eyes, the serpent's bite of the following verses — and it still addresses the drunkard as a man who tarries long at the wine, who seeks mixed wine, and who must look away.

The principle to recover is Proverbs 23:31. The command is placed at the eye, before the lip. Scripture does not forbid wine, which it elsewhere calls a gift that maketh glad the heart of man; it forbids the long tarrying and the seeking, and it sets the drunkard's own face before him as evidence.
roots_summary: Saxon read, red; renders Hebrew chaklilil, dark-flashing or bloodshot, of the drunkard's eyes at Proverbs 23:29.

pos: n. (vomiting; the act of casting up from the stomach)
etymology: Saxon spiwan, to vomit, cognate with Latin spuere, to spit. In Habakkuk 2:16 it renders the Hebrew qiqalon, shame or disgrace, with the sense of vomit.
biblical_def: The fourth woe of Habakkuk 2 falls on the man who makes his neighbour drunk in order to look on his nakedness (Habakkuk 2:15). The sentence answers the crime in kind: “Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the LORD'S right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory” (Habakkuk 2:16). Babylon had passed the bottle to the nations and stripped them while they were insensible. Now Babylon drinks, and from the LORD's own right hand, and the glory she boasted in is covered with her own vomit. The Authorized Version uses spewing once. The image is deliberately repulsive and the dictionary does not soften it: Scripture uses the body's most degrading involuntary act to picture what happens to imperial glory under divine judgment. The cup of the LORD's right hand runs through the prophets and into Revelation, and it is always this — the wine of wrath given to those who gave it to others. What a man pours out he will drink.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SPEWING, noun The act of vomiting; that which is vomited.
webster_full: SPEW, verb transitive To vomit; to puke; to eject from the stomach.
2. To eject with loathing; to cast forth with abhorrence.
SPEWING, participle present tense Vomiting; ejecting from the stomach.
SPEWING, noun The act of vomiting.
SPEWY, adjective Wet; foggy; moist.
scriptures: Hab 2:16
Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the LORD'S right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory.
Hab 2:15
Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness!
The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation;
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The only common handling of this verse is avoidance. Habakkuk 2:16 is considered too coarse to read aloud, and so the fourth woe is skipped. Scripture chose the image, and it chose it to make imperial glory contemptible. A dictionary that honours the Authorized Version prints the word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is retribution in kind. Babylon made the nations drunk and looked on their shame; Babylon drinks from the LORD's right hand and her own glory is fouled. Revelation 14:10 carries the same cup into the last judgment.

pos: v. (participle of swell; distended, as a limb from venom)
etymology: Saxon swellan, to swell. In Acts 28:6 it renders the Greek pimprasthai, to be inflamed or to swell up.
biblical_def: Paul has been shipwrecked on Melita, and a viper fastens on his hand as he gathers sticks. The islanders draw the obvious conclusion and wait: “Howbeit they looked when he should have swollen, or fallen down dead suddenly: but after they had looked a great while, and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god” (Acts 28:6). The verse is a model of Luke's plain reporting. The swelling was expected because that is what viper venom does; the absence of swelling was observed over time, not assumed; and the barbarians' theology swung from murderer to god in the space of an hour. The Authorized Version uses swollen once. Two doctrines sit in it. First, the promise of Mark 16:18 is fulfilled in the ordinary way — Paul shook off the beast and felt no harm (Acts 28:5) — without Paul ever having tested God by handling the snake on purpose. Second, a miracle does not produce sound doctrine: the islanders moved from one superstition to another, and Paul had still to preach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SWOLLEN, participle passive of swell. Increased in bulk; distended; inflamed.
webster_full: SWOLLEN, SWOLN, participle passive of swell.
SWELL, verb intransitive To grow larger; to dilate or extend the exterior surface or dimensions of a body.
2. To increase in size or extent by any addition.
3. To rise or be driven into waves or billows.
4. To be inflated; to belly; as swelling sails.
scriptures: Act 28:6

Howbeit they looked when he should have swollen, or fallen down dead suddenly: but after they had looked a great while, and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.
Act 28:5
And he shook off the beast into the fire, and felt no harm.
And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is charismatic. Acts 28 is cited as warrant for deliberate snake-handling, as though Mark 16:18 were an invitation to test God. Paul did not pick up the viper; it fastened on him while he was gathering firewood for cold, wet shipwreck survivors. A promise of preservation in the path of duty is not a licence to leave the path.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that signs do not convert. The islanders watched a genuine miracle and concluded that Paul was a god, which is exactly the error he had rebuked at Lystra (Acts 14:15). Faith comes by hearing, not by watching for swelling.

pos: adj. (full of pain; grievous; here, too hard to bear or to understand)
etymology: From pain, French peine, Latin poena, punishment, with the ending -ful. In Psalm 73:16 it renders a Hebrew word for trouble or labour.
biblical_def: Asaph has watched the wicked prosper until his own feet almost slipped, and he tries to think his way out of it: “When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me” (Psalm 73:16). The Authorized Version uses painful once, and it uses it of intellectual and spiritual labour, not of bodily hurt. The problem of the prosperity of the ungodly cannot be solved by reasoning at a desk; Asaph tried and it broke him. What ends the psalm's crisis is a change of place: “Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end” (Psalm 73:17). He did not get a new argument. He went where God is worshipped, and from there he saw where the wicked were going. The dictionary reads this as a standing rebuke to the private wrestle. A believer tormented by providence is not helped by more thinking in isolation; he is helped by the house of God, the preached word, and the company of the saints. Asaph's conclusion follows: “But it is good for me to draw near to God” (Psalm 73:28). The painful thing became plain in the sanctuary and nowhere else.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PAINFUL, adjective Full of pain; giving pain; distressing; also, requiring labor; difficult.
webster_full: PAINFUL, adjective Full of pain; producing uneasiness or distress, either to the body or mind.
2. Requiring labor or toil; difficult; executed with laborious effort.
3. Laborious; exercising much labor; industrious.
PAINFULLY, adverb With pain or affliction; laboriously.
PAINFULNESS, noun Affliction; sorrow; grief; also, industry; laborious effort.
scriptures: When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me;
Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end.
But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord GOD, that I may declare all thy works.
corruption_summary: Spiritual crisis is now a matter for private processing; Psalm 73 is resolved in the sanctuary of God, not in the psalmist's own head.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic instinct sends the doubting believer inward — to journalling, to reflection, to naming his feelings. Asaph had already tried the inward route, and his verdict on it is this verse: it was too painful for me. The psalm does not reward introspection; it rescues the psalmist out of it.

The principle to recover is the ordinary means of grace. He went into the sanctuary of God, and there understood their end. Public worship, the word preached, the fellowship of the saints — these are where God has promised to meet troubled believers, and they are not a supplement to private struggle but the answer to it.

pos: n. pl. (loud cries of anguish; groanings uttered aloud)
etymology: Saxon rarian, to roar or bellow. In Job 3:24 it renders the Hebrew she'agah, the roar of a lion, used of a man's cry.
biblical_def: Job breaks a week's silence and the first thing out of him is not argument but noise: “For my sighing cometh before I eat, and my roarings are poured out like the waters” (Job 3:24). The Hebrew word is the lion's roar. Scripture is not embarrassed by it. A righteous man under the hand of God made a sound like a beast, and the Holy Spirit recorded it in the canon. The next verse tells why: “For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me” (Job 3:25). Nothing in the psalms or the prophets requires the sufferer to be composed. David uses the same root of himself — “my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long” (Psalm 32:3) — though there the roaring was the fruit of unconfessed sin, while Job's is the cry of an upright man in the furnace. The Authorized Version uses roarings once. The dictionary notes the pastoral consequence: lament is a biblical genre, it is loud, and it is not unbelief. Job roars in chapter 3 and says in chapter 13 that though God slay him, yet will he trust in Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ROARING, noun A loud cry; the cry of a beast; outcry of distress.
webster_full: ROAR, verb intransitive To cry with a full loud sound; to utter a deep loud sound, as a lion or other beast.
2. To utter a loud cry of distress; as, to roar for anguish.
3. To make a loud noise, as the wind or the sea.
ROARING, noun A loud cry, as of a beast or of a man in distress.
2. The loud noise of the sea or of the wind.
scriptures: Job 3:24
For my sighing cometh before I eat, and my roarings are poured out like the waters.
Job 3:25
For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me.
Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
corruption_summary: Loud grief is treated either as a symptom to be medicated or as weak faith; Scripture gives it a canonical voice.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors squeeze the sufferer. The first is therapeutic and treats the roaring as pathology only, to be quieted. The second is pious and treats it as unbelief, to be rebuked. Job 3 is in the canon, Lamentations is in the canon, and a third of the psalter is complaint. God has given His people words for the worst days, and they are loud words.

The principle to recover is the shape of biblical lament: it roars, and it still trusts. Job 3:24 and Job 13:15 are the same man. Grief that is honest with God is not the opposite of faith; the counterfeit is the silence of Psalm 32:3, where unconfessed sin left David roaring all the day long with nothing said to God at all.

pos: n. pl. (arguments urged in a cause; the speech of one who pleads)
etymology: French plaider, to plead, from Latin placitum, a decree or plea. In Job 13:6 it renders the Hebrew rib, a legal controversy or suit.
biblical_def: Job turns from his comforters to address them as a defendant addresses a court: “Hear now my reasoning, and hearken to the pleadings of my lips” (Job 13:6). The whole book is cast as a lawsuit, and the Hebrew word here is the word for a legal dispute. Job is not venting; he is pleading a cause, and he intends to plead it before God Himself — “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him” (Job 13:15). The Authorized Version uses pleadings once. The dictionary notes the astonishing liberty Scripture grants here. A creature may bring his case; he may argue; he may say he does not understand and insist on his integrity against false accusation — and God, at the end of the book, rebukes the three friends and not Job for what they said of Him. What Job may not do is win. The answer out of the whirlwind does not refute his pleadings; it shows him the Pleader he needs, and the New Testament names Him: one Mediator between God and men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PLEADING, noun The act of advocating any cause; the written statements of parties in a cause.
webster_full: PLEAD, verb intransitive To argue in support of a claim, or in defense against the claim of another.
2. To urge reasons for or against; to attempt to persuade by argument or supplication.
3. In law, to present an answer to the declaration of the plaintiff.
PLEADING, noun The act of advocating any cause.
PLEADINGS, noun plural The mutual altercations between the plaintiff and defendant.
scriptures: Job 13:6
Hear now my reasoning, and hearken to the pleadings of my lips.
Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The misreading to name is the pious one that makes Job's pleadings sinful presumption. God's own verdict is against that reading: the LORD tells Eliphaz that he and his two friends have not spoken of Him the thing that is right, as His servant Job hath. Job's pleadings were honest and were accepted; the friends' theology was tidy and was rebuked.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer's case is pleaded by Another. Job longed for a daysman betwixt him and God; 1 Timothy 2:5 names Him, and the pleadings of our lips are answered in the intercession of the one Mediator.

pos: n. pl. (habitual dealings; here, covetous schemes)
etymology: Greek praktikos, from prassein, to do, through Latin practicare. In 2 Peter 2:14 it stands in the phrase covetous practices, Greek pleonexia.
biblical_def: Peter's portrait of the false teacher is unsparing: “Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin; beguiling unstable souls: an heart they have exercised with covetous practices; cursed children” (2 Peter 2:14). The word exercised is the athletic word — trained, drilled, brought by repetition to competence. These men have practised covetousness until they are good at it. The Authorized Version uses practices once, and it belongs to a verse about habit. Sin here is not an occasional fall but an acquired skill, and the apostle names the pattern it follows: “Which have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness” (2 Peter 2:15). Balaam is the archetype — a man with a genuine prophetic gift who priced it. The dictionary notes that Peter aims this at teachers inside the church, not at the world outside it. Covetous practice in a pulpit beguiles unstable souls, and the apostle's word for the practitioners is cursed children.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PRACTICE, noun Frequent or customary actions; a succession of acts of a similar kind; habit.
webster_full: PRACTICE, noun Frequent or customary actions; a succession of acts of a similar kind or in a like employment.
2. Use; customary use.
3. Dexterity acquired by use.
4. Actual performance; distinguished from theory.
5. Medical treatment of diseases; also, the exercise of any profession.
scriptures: Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin; beguiling unstable souls: an heart they have exercised with covetous practices; cursed children:
Which have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness;
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
corruption_summary: Sin as practised skill has largely dropped out of modern preaching; so has the apostolic naming of covetous teachers.
corruption_paragraphs: Two things have gone soft. The first is the doctrine of habit: Peter says the heart is exercised, trained, drilled in covetousness, which is why the man cannot cease from sin. Modern treatment prefers incidents to patterns, and so never addresses the training. The second is the willingness to name teachers. Peter does it in the plainest terms available to him — cursed children, following the way of Balaam.

The principle to recover is 1 Timothy 6:10. The love of money is a root, not a branch, and men have erred from the faith by coveting after it. A ministry that has made covetousness a practised skill will beguile unstable souls whatever its doctrine on paper.

pos: adv. (emptily; to no purpose; without ground)
etymology: Latin vanus, empty, through French vain, with the ending -ly. In Colossians 2:18 it renders the Greek eike, without cause or ground.
biblical_def: Paul warns the Colossians against a devout-looking error: “Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind” (Colossians 2:18). Every term is chosen. The humility is voluntary — self-chosen, not commanded; the worship is directed to angels; the teacher intrudes into what he has not seen; and the result is a man swollen with nothing. Vainly puffed up is the apostle's judgment on asceticism and mystical speculation together: the inflation is real and the content is empty. The Authorized Version uses vainly once. The next verse gives the fatal defect: “And not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God” (Colossians 2:19). That is the test the dictionary applies to every spirituality offered to Christians — angelic hierarchies, visionary experience, self-imposed severity, or the modern varieties. Does it hold the Head? If it does not, the growth is swelling, not increase.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): VAINLY, adverb In vain; to no purpose; ineffectually; idly; foolishly.
webster_full: VAINLY, adverb In vain; to no purpose; ineffectually.
2. Idly; foolishly.
3. Proudly; arrogantly.
VAIN, adjective Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance.
2. Fruitless; ineffectual; as, all our efforts were vain.
scriptures: Col 2:18
Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
Col 2:19
And not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not to any honour of the satisfying of the flesh.
corruption_summary: Self-chosen severity and visionary experience are still marketed as depth; Paul calls them empty inflation that does not hold the Head.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 2:18 describes a permanent species of error, and its modern forms are easy to name: contemplative techniques imported from outside Scripture, angel-devotion, claimed visions and private revelations, graded severities of diet and discipline presented as spiritual advancement. Verse 23 grants that such things have indeed a shew of wisdom. A shew is all they have.

The principle to recover is verse 19. Growth in the Christian life comes through the Head, by joints and bands, in the body — that is, through Christ by ordinary means in the church. Anything that advertises increase while loosening the grip on Christ is producing swelling, and Paul's word for it is vainly puffed up.

etymology: Saxon raesc, hasty, with the ending -ly. In Acts 19:36 it renders the Greek propetes, falling forward, headlong.
biblical_def: The riot at Ephesus is quieted not by an apostle but by a pagan magistrate. The townclerk reminds the mob of their own civic religion and then says: “Seeing then that these things cannot be spoken against, ye ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rashly” (Acts 19:36). The Greek is the word for falling forward — headlong, unbalanced, moving faster than judgment. Paul's companions had been dragged into the theatre, Paul himself was restrained from entering, and two hours of shouting had produced nothing but noise. The Authorized Version uses rashly once, and it is worth noting who says it. Luke records that the mob was dispersed by the ordinary machinery of civil order: a magistrate pointing to the courts and the lawful assembly. The dictionary reads this as a plain instance of the civil sphere doing its God-ordained work. The state is not the church, but it bears the sword to restrain violence, and a townclerk who keeps a mob from murder is doing God's business whether he knows it or not.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The reading to resist is the one that makes the Ephesian townclerk a hero of tolerance, as though the lesson were that religious passion should always be cooled. Luke's point is narrower and better: a lawful magistrate restrained an unlawful mob. The clerk's own speech is full of idolatry; his office was still doing its proper work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lawful distinction of spheres. Romans 13:4 gives the magistrate the sword to restrain evil; the church has the word and the keys. The riot at Ephesus was stopped by the first, and the gospel had already been advanced by the second.
